records.name: Saint Barthélemy
records.summary:
Under the metropolitan civil law that governs this collectivity: same-sex marriage since 2013, gender-identity anti-discrimination protections, surgery-free legal gender change, gender-affirming care available for decades, and the state's 2023 conversion-practice ban — no legal restriction touches trans or same-sex visitors, and a rights-rating page scores the territory among the region's strongest frameworks with the caveat that non-binary recognition is absent and healthcare capacity is tiny.

Visitor-facing evidence is unusually direct: verified 2026 destination guides describe a discreet luxury culture — full legal protections, 'a cosmopolitan crowd that genuinely doesn't care', no organised scene but complete safety for same-sex couples — and the rights overview reports the island attracts trans residents from less accepting neighbours. A current-status review tempers that surface: local acceptance runs lower than the visitor economy implies, though no legal regression exists. The only documented adverse mechanism remains the framework-wide prison findings. Read: protected and comfortable, shallow community depth, care requires travel.

sources.claim: BuzzFeed News feature (Jan 2018, in French context): trans women in France incarcerated on the basis of their legal gender fall into a legal gray area and are punished beyond their alleged crimes - relevant to Saint Barthélemy as a French overseas collectivity applying French law.

Opinion of 25 May 2021 by France's Contrôleur général des lieux de privation de liberté (CGLPL) on the treatment of transgender persons in places of deprivation of liberty: based on ~40 referrals since 2010, it finds serious violations of fundamental rights persist across places of detention, with recommendations applicable also to intersex and non-binary persons.

Grokipedia article on transgender rights in Saint Barthélemy: French national law applies - legal gender-marker change without surgery/sterilization (2016 reform), gender-affirming care available since 1975, anti-discrimination protections extended to gender identity; no non-binary recognition; reported to attract trans migrants from Guadeloupe and Martinique seeking a more accepting environment; healthcare access limited by the territory's small size.

Gayborhood destination guide (verified April 2026): St Barth as a discreet luxury destination - 'full French legal protections', a cosmopolitan crowd that 'genuinely doesn't care', no organised gay scene but a completely safe environment for same-sex couples; Traven-Dex safety score 8.6.

Agtra (Against Transphobia) country page for Saint Barthélemy: trans-rights overview scoring 7.7/10 - legal gender change without surgery (per French law, since 2017), judicial process possibly involving medical evaluation, no non-binary recognition, same-sex marriage legal since May 2013, anti-discrimination laws in place, limited local healthcare access; no government LGBT travel advice; no trans-specific community travel advice submitted.
Out Of Office gay travel agency blog: 'Is St Barths gay friendly?' - travel-agency perspective marketing the island as a welcoming luxury destination for gay couples.

freshness.fact: French framework applies: marriage equality, anti-discrimination law and the 2023 conversion-practice ban; local acceptance lower, no legal regression.

records.name: Belarus
records.summary:
Belarus is a place trans visitors should avoid entirely. In 2024 the authorities escalated from hostility to active persecution: a Culture Ministry decree reclassified transgender identity itself — "the desire to live and be seen by others as a person of an opposite sex" — as pornography, punishable by up to four years in prison. In September 2024 a wave of arrests targeted the community: TG House Belarus documented over 15 LGBTQ+ people detained, including at least eight transgender people, several arrested for merely subscribing to "extremist" resources online.

Detained trans people were beaten and forced to record humiliating "confession videos" circulated on pro-government channels. ODIHR's 2024 reporting notes the majority of bias incidents in Belarus targeted trans people, including "physical assaults, threats, abductions, humiliation, and coerced confessions related to their gender identity by law enforcement officers." State media runs systematic dehumanising propaganda.

Gender transition technically remains legal, but the 2024 pornography decree means a discoverable online presence or simply living visibly as trans can be prosecuted. For a visitor: no documented trans-tourist case yet, but police actively hunt trans people, any visible gender nonconformity risks detention, and foreign nationals receive no protection.

sources.claim: Human Rights Watch (Apr 2024): 'Belarus Calls LGBT Lives 'Pornography'' — authorities treat depictions of LGBT life as banned 'pornography', extending repression of LGBT people.

JURIST (Sept 2024): TG House Belarus reported that 15+ LGBTQ individuals, including eight trans people, were detained within a month across several cities for allegedly subscribing to 'extremist resources'; most trans detainees were charged with hooliganism, two with pornography. Detainees reported physical and psychological abuse, and some fled the country. The Prosecutor General had announced in February a bill to punish 'promotion of non-traditional relationships'.

OSCE/ODIHR 2024 Hate Crime Report for Belarus: Belarus has not reported hate-crime data to ODIHR since 2015 and has no National Point of Contact; civil-society reports for 2024 came from Human Constanta and others. No official data available.
AP: 'Activists say police in Belarus beat LGBTQ+ people while arresting and charging them' — rights groups report beatings, coerced charges and expanding 'LGBT propaganda' repression.

ILGA-Europe Annual Review 2025 (covering 2024) chapter on Belarus: state TV equated LGBTI identities with paedophilia and called them 'a weapon in the hands of the West'; TG House recorded increased hate speech in state propaganda; the Prosecutor General's Office plans an administrative-penalty law against 'LGBTI propaganda' (not yet tabled); at least ten trans people left Belarus in a year due to discrimination and repression; a new National Security Concept emphasises 'traditional values'.

ILGA World Treaty Bodies Strategic Litigation Toolkit, Part 2 - Case Digest (2024): compilation of UN Treaty Body decisions on 25 SOGIESC cases (criminalisation, asylum, violence, expression, families, legal gender recognition) - includes jurisprudence relevant to Belarus among other states.

US State Department 1999 Human Rights Report for Belarus (archived): historical baseline - documents the legal and social situation including treatment of homosexuality under the Lukashenka government.

Report 'Are all equal before the law?' (Bortnik & Sementsov, citing Amnesty International 2006-2007 context): Belarus's constitutional equality guarantee (Article 22) versus reality - clampdown on civil society, harassment of activists, arbitrary detentions, death penalty retained; the legal and political climate facing LGBT people in Belarus.

freshness.fact: April 2026 law criminalises 'propaganda of homosexual relations, gender reassignment, childlessness' — a new enforcement layer post-dating every cited 2024-25 source; acts remain legal, zero protections.

records.name: Belize
records.summary: Belize demands real caution. The Court of Appeal struck down the sodomy law in 2016 (Orozco v AG) — the Caribbean's first decriminalisation ruling; Belize has an organised community (UNIBAM) and anti-discrimination employment protection. No LGR; gang violence in Belize City is a general risk.

sources.claim: NOTE: Not retrievable at research time (HTTP 403); the underlying Human Dignity Trust page documents constitutional challenges to laws criminalising same-sex activity across the Eastern Caribbean, including Belize (the 2016 Orozco ruling decriminalised same-sex conduct in Belize).

Erasing 76 Crimes (Nov 2018): Belize's turnaround on gay rights - accepted 15 of 17 SOGI recommendations at its UPR (first CARICOM country to accept that many), after decriminalising in 2016; activist Caleb Orozco describes the 180-degree turn in the state's SOGI position.
Washington Blade (Aug 2016): Belize's top court strikes down the sodomy law.

Central America living guide (April 2019): 'Is Belize gay-friendly?' - local writer on improving conditions; the 2016 decriminalisation (first former British Caribbean colony to overturn its anti-sodomy law); tourism has long been gay-friendly (1998 gay cruise protests vs 2009 welcomed lesbian cruise); Caleb Orozco's constitutional challenge and UNIBAM's work.

Erasing 76 Crimes (May 2013): courtroom coverage of the Orozco constitutional challenge to Section 53 (the anti-sodomy law) - live-tweeted dispatches from psychologist Asa DeMatteo describing the arguments on constitutional fundamental rights versus church intervenors.

records.name: Bermuda
records.summary:
Bermuda decriminalised private adult same-sex conduct in 1994 (House of Assembly, 22-16) and in 2013 outlawed discrimination on grounds of sexual orientation. Same-sex marriages performed in 2017 were withdrawn the following year by a Domestic Partnership Act — the first jurisdiction anywhere to reverse marriage equality — and in March 2022 the Judicial Committee of the Privy Council upheld that restoration of the traditional-marriage definition, so partnerships, not marriage, are the available status for same-sex couples.

For a transgender visitor the more telling fact is the protection gap: there is no legal recognition of transgender people, and therefore no gender-identity-specific discrimination protection at all. Church influence is significant in local politics — when a prominent entertainer's gay-charity cruise sought to dock in 2007 the premier's colourful defence was needed against religious objections — and the tourism economy that the island depends on has repeatedly had to be pointed at inclusivity.

sources.claim: Bernews (Feb 2018): Bermuda's Governor gave assent to the Domestic Partnership Act 2017, replacing same-sex marriage with domestic partnerships for both same-sex and heterosexual couples - the reversal that made Bermuda the first jurisdiction to revoke marriage equality.

PinkNews (April 2007): Bermuda's Premier Ewart Brown defended allowing Rosie O'Donnell's gay family cruise to dock against church objections ('If we discriminate against a cruise ship, then we would have to send a homosexual detection unit to the airport') - documents tourism-related LGBT friction.

LGBTQ Nation/AP (July 2013): Bermuda's Senate passed the Human Rights Amendment Act outlawing discrimination on grounds of sexual orientation (also banning age discrimination); same-sex marriage not then permitted.
Royal Gazette (May 1994): Bermuda's House of Assembly voted 22-16 to decriminalise sex between adult males, removing two Criminal Code sections - historical legal context.

records.name: Bolivia
records.summary:
Bolivia is workable for trans visitors — one of Latin America's legal pioneers on paper. The 2016 Gender Identity Law was ground-breaking: legal gender recognition on the basis of self-declared identity (administrative process, no surgery), and gender identity is an explicitly protected ground in anti-discrimination law. Bolivia's constitution also names gender identity.

Implementation lags the statute: the first national LGBTQ+ survey (2024) reveals significant exclusion in health, education, employment, and housing; social conservatism is strong outside La Paz/Santa Cruz; and bureaucrats often resist applying the Gender Identity Law. There is no documented pattern of police targeting of trans people as such, and no traveler-facing restriction — but also limited effective protection outside major cities.

sources.claim: Comparative Politics article (April 2024) 'Activists, Parties, and the Expansion of Trans Rights in Bolivia': Bolivia prohibits gender-identity discrimination and passed a ground-breaking gender identity law (2016, allowing name/marker change) despite low voter support; trans activists leveraged access to ruling-party legislators; contradictory heteronormative laws passed alongside because both organised religion and LGBT activists were party constituents.

NOTE: Not retrievable at research time (WordPress critical error); the underlying Agencia Presentes article (Dec 2024) covers Bolivia's first virtual survey revealing the great exclusion of LGBTI people.

US State Department 2011 Human Rights Report for Bolivia: general human-rights assessment (arbitrary deprivation of life, prison conditions, corruption) - the LGBT section documents the constitutional anti-discrimination guarantee and societal discrimination.

Newsweek (July 2017): Trump's transgender military ban leaves the US off a short list of countries that do not legally discriminate on gender identity in the armed forces - comparative context including Bolivia's military policy.

Geneva Foundation for Medical Education and Research, Bolivia sexual and reproductive rights page: the Constitution prohibits discrimination based on sexual orientation and gender identity (Article 14(II)) and guarantees sexual rights (Article 66); documents the legal framework including abortion law.

eju.tv/La Razón (Aug 2014, in Spanish): gay military personnel in Bolivia's armed forces live between discrimination and clandestinity - a soldier's hidden relationship with a captain; the TLGB collective and human-rights defenders call for openness in the institution.

freshness.fact: Post-2017 developments the archived sources miss: Jan-2018 Inter-American Court opinion; Dec-2020 civil-registry 'free union' recognition; 2016 gender-identity law remains a world-leading baseline. 2024 article still current.

records.name: Brazil
records.summary:
Brazil combines some of the world's strongest legal protections for transgender people with a high level of real-world violence — the classic gap between law and practice. Courts allow name and gender-marker changes without surgery, the Supreme Court has criminalised transphobia (making it punishable like racism), courts fine businesses that discriminate, and official guidance affirms trans people's right to use bathrooms matching their identity.

For visitors, big-city queer life is vibrant and highly visible — São Paulo hosts the world's largest Pride parade — and the law is unambiguously on a trans traveller's side. The practical risks are concentrated in nightlife and app-based meetings: a majority of physical violence against LGBTQIA+ people in São Paulo happens at night, and robbery schemes luring gay men via dating apps have been fatal.

Exercise particular caution after dark, with nightlife and app meetings, and in peripheral areas. Violence against local trans people (Brazil records the world's highest absolute toll) is heavily concentrated in poor and marginalised communities, not tourist areas.

sources.claim: Wikipedia overview of LGBTQ rights in Brazil: covers the 2018 Supreme Court rulings on gender identity (self-declaration of gender marker; name/gender change without surgery), non-binary recognition, healthcare, conversion-therapy ban, anti-LGBT violence, and social conditions. Same-sex marriage recognised since 2013.

Outright International country overview (updated March 2026): marriage equality since 2013 (with congressional repeal efforts underway); 2019 Supreme Court ruling prohibits discrimination and hate crimes based on SOGI; trans people can change gender markers by self-determination. Brazil continues to have one of the highest rates of violence against sexual and gender minorities, particularly trans people; 3,000+ openly LGBTQ candidates ran in the 2024 municipal elections.

Brazilian law firm guide (April 2026) for expats: same-sex marriage, spousal visa equality, adoption, and name/gender-marker changes are available; notes Brazil has no comprehensive federal anti-discrimination statute, with protections built from court rulings.

Agência Pública (May 2024, in Portuguese): investigation into violence against LGBTQIA+ people in São Paulo nightlife - 57% of physical-violence incidents against LGBTQIA+ people in the capital occurred at night; victims report insecurity in bars and clubs.

AP (Oct 2024): 'Death threats assail Brazil's trailblazing trans candidates as they campaign' — nearly 1,000 transgender politicians run in municipal elections across every state amid threats and intimidation, as the number of trans officeholders has tripled since the last cycle.

ConJur (May 2025, in Portuguese): São Paulo Court of Justice upheld a moral-damages award against a nightclub that barred a trans woman for wearing feminine clothing ('bustiê e minissaia'); the court held trans people have the right to treatment conforming to their social identity and raised the compensation to R$10,000.

Latinoamérica21 (2022): Brazil's Superior Court of Justice unanimously held that the Maria da Penha Law (domestic-violence protection) applies to transgender women, based on gender rather than biological sex - after lower courts had twice denied protection to a trans woman attacked by her father.

São Paulo Municipal Council: official page of the Parliamentary Inquiry Commission (CPI) on Violence Against Trans and Travesti People — its remit, members, hearings and final report on lethal violence against trans people in the municipality.

Government of Canada travel advice for Brazil (updated Aug 2026): 'Exercise a high degree of caution' with regional advisories; covers safety, entry/exit, health, laws and culture. General travel advice, not trans-specific.

Intrepid Travel country guide: calls Brazil 'progressive' on LGBTQIA+ rights — marriage equality, same-sex adoption and anti-discrimination laws in employment and housing — while noting an active anti-LGBTQIA+ minority and one of the world's highest murder rates of LGBTQIA+ people.

Brazzil magazine (March 2000): historian James N. Green on 'Pleasures in the Parks of Rio de Janeiro during the Brazilian Belle Époque, 1898-1914' - historical account of male same-sex cruising and sexual culture in Rio, documenting the long history of homosexuality in Brazil.

freshness.fact: Marriage/adoption since 2013 and STF ruling equating SO/GI-discrimination to racism (2019) remain the framework; trans-inclusion provisions in violence-prevention law not reversed. Cited overview still matches current law.

records.name: Barbados
records.summary: Barbados demands real caution. Courts struck down the buggery laws in 2022; Barbados has an organised community (Equals, B-GLAD) and a functioning state. No LGR; modest social conservatism; tourist areas accustomed to diverse visitors.

sources.claim: NOTE: Not retrievable at research time (HTTP 403); the underlying Human Dignity Trust page documents Eastern Caribbean constitutional challenges; Barbados decriminalised same-sex conduct in December 2022 via such a constitutional challenge.

NOTE: This HRW article is about Antigua and Barbuda's 2022 ruling, not Barbados specifically; included as Eastern Caribbean regional context (Barbados's own High Court struck down its buggery and indecency laws the same year).

Erasing 76 Crimes (Nov 2018): first-person account by Barbadian trans activist Alexa Hoffmann - the country's first Transgender Day of Remembrance vigil; rising trans murder rates globally (369 reported in 2018); her own brush with death; notes 62% of trans murder victims are sex workers and misgendering of victims as 'cross-dressers'.

Erasing 76 Crimes (April 2019): the man who attacked Alexa Hoffmann with a meat cleaver (Feb 2018, serious injuries including to her throat) was ordered to pay BD$460 (~US$230) or serve three months - effectively no jail time; Hoffmann led Barbados's first Pride (2017) and is lead claimant in the challenge to the anti-sodomy law (life imprisonment, 'worst in the Western Hemisphere').

Erasing 76 Crimes commentary (Aug 2020) by Alexa Hoffmann: Barbados's Employment (Protection from Discrimination) Bill 2020 omitted gender identity - trans people are frequently denied or fired from jobs for 'dressing wrong'; Hoffmann herself was terminated by a law firm after legally changing her name; the 'Welcome Stamp' remote-worker visa is tainted by discriminatory laws.

Daily Xtra (June 2018): Barbadian activists (Alexa Hoffmann as trans woman claimant, with Canadian support) filed the first challenge to Barbados's Sexual Offences Act at the Inter-American Commission on Human Rights - the law puts trans people in legal jeopardy and enables prejudice and violence.

records.name: Brunei
records.summary:
Brunei's Sharia Penal Code contains one of the world's most explicit trans-specific criminal provisions: Section 198 creates an offence of "a man posing as a woman or vice versa", and the Bruneian government has confirmed in its official guidance that the code applies to all persons in the country including tourists — travel agents are briefed accordingly. A separate indecency provision criminalises clothing that "tarnishes the image of Islam" with fines and imprisonment, and same-sex intimacy carries a stoning sentence (under a formal moratorium since 2019, with whipping and long prison terms actively available).

Enforcement is quiet rather than predatory — no prosecution of a foreign visitor under these provisions has been documented — but the country is an absolute monarchy with heavy surveillance, censorship, and no LGBT organising of any kind, and LGBT Bruneians have fled abroad. The legal exposure for a discovered trans visitor is categorical: no recognition, no protection, and gender expression itself is a written offence.

sources.claim: NOTE: Not retrievable at research time (HTTP 403); the underlying document is the text of Brunei's Penal Code (hosted by the Norwegian government), including the Syariah Penal Code provisions.

NOTE: Not retrievable at research time (HTTP 403); the underlying Human Dignity Trust briefing (April 2019) analyses Brunei's implementation of the Syariah Penal Code Order 2013, including death by stoning for anal sex and adultery.

BBC (April 2019): Brunei implemented strict new Islamic penal provisions making anal sex and adultery punishable by stoning to death, theft by amputation; homosexuality was already illegal (up to 10 years). Brunei's gay community expressed shock and fear; the Sultan called for 'stronger' Islamic teachings. No execution has been carried out since 1957; the law mostly applies to Muslims.

AP (Apr 2019): 'Brunei death penalty moratorium applied to new Shariah laws' — the sultan says the capital-punishment moratorium covers the new Shariah penal code allowing stoning for gay sex and adultery; under the prior law homosexuality was already punishable by up to 10 years.
NOTE: Not retrievable at research time (HTTP 403); the underlying France24 piece (April 2019) covers the fear gripping Brunei's gay community after the Sharia penal code came into force.

TIME (April 2019): first-person reporting on what it is like to be gay in Brunei after homosexuality became punishable by stoning to death under the new Sharia penal code; describes the climate of fear in the small sultanate.

UK House of Commons Library debate pack (April 2019) on LGBT rights in Brunei: the Syariah Penal Code Order 2013 (in force in stages, final stage 3 April 2019) requires death by stoning for extramarital sex, anal sex and abortion; 40 lashes for lesbian sex; amputation for theft. HRW called it 'barbaric'; the UN High Commissioner urged Brunei to halt it.
NOTE: Not retrievable at research time (HTTP 403); the underlying SSRN paper relates to Brunei's Sharia penal code.

HRW '#OUTLAWED' global map feature: at least 67 countries criminalise same-sex relations and at least nine criminalise forms of gender expression. Notes that among countries expressly forbidding trans expression, Brunei and Oman have national laws criminalising 'posing as' or 'imitating' a person of a different sex.

US State Department 2017 Human Rights Report for Brunei: official assessment covering the Sharia Penal Code's provisions (including death by stoning for anal sex/adultery, 40 lashes for lesbian sex), enforcement practices, and societal treatment - the report covers the period after international condemnation led Brunei to announce a moratorium on the death penalty for the code.

freshness.fact: Syariah Penal Code order (2019) still in force: death penalty de jure for male same-sex conduct, de facto whipping/imprisonment; 2019 moratorium reported intact. 2019 sources remain the accurate statement of law.
